faq.a: The tapetum lucidum, Latin for bright carpet, is a reflective layer at the back of the eye in many animals. It sends light back through the retina, helping them see in dim light.
asks: What is the mirror in a cat's eye?

faq.q: Do cats' eyes make their own light?
faq.a: No. Cats' eyes only reflect light that shines into them, like a car headlight or torch. In total darkness their eyes do not glow.
asks: Do cats' eyes glow in total darkness?

faq.q: How do cats see in the dark?
faq.a: Cats have huge pupils, lots of light-sensitive rod cells and a tapetum that gives light a second pass. Together these let them see in far dimmer light than we can, though not in total darkness.
asks: Can cats see in complete darkness?
Why are cats good at night vision?

faq.q: Why do people get red eyes in flash photos?
faq.a: Humans have no tapetum. A camera flash lights up the blood-rich back of the eye, and that red light reflects straight back into the lens, giving red-eye.
asks: Why don't human eyes glow like cats' eyes?

faq.a: Dogs, foxes, deer, cows, horses, crocodiles and many deep-sea fish have a tapetum. Eyeshine colour varies: green, yellow, blue or even red.
asks: Why do deer eyes glow in headlights?

facts: Tapetum lucidum is Latin for bright carpet or shining layer.
Humans lack a tapetum lucidum; red-eye in flash photos is light reflected from the blood-rich back of the eye.
Many night-active animals, including dogs, deer and crocodiles, have a tapetum and show eyeshine.
